youtube.aciklama:
The Eustachian tube connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx. In this lesson we cover its bony and cartilaginous parts, the muscles that open it, and its ventilation, drainage and protection functions. We also look at how it differs in children, its dysfunctions and how it is assessed in the clinic.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Bluestone, Eustachian Tube: Structure, Function, Role in Otitis Media; Gray's Anatomy; Katz, Handbook of Clinical Audiology; Gelfand, Essentials of Audiology.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

sahneler.alt: Anatomy, functions and differences in children
cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will examine the channel that connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx: the Eustachian tube.
We will learn its structure, how it opens and closes, its three main functions, and why it causes problems more easily in children.

sahneler.baslik: From the middle ear to the *nasopharynx*
cumleler: The channel leaving the anterior wall of the middle ear is anatomically called the tuba auditiva, the Eustachian tube.

cumleler.yazi: It is named after Bartolomeo Eustachi, the sixteenth-century Italian anatomist who described it.
The tube connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx, the upper part of the throat behind the nose.

cumleler: In adults it is about thirty six millimeters long.
It runs forward, medially and downward from the middle ear; its opening in the nasopharynx is lower than its opening in the middle ear.
Its opening in the nasopharynx lies on the lateral wall and is surrounded by a cartilaginous bulge.
Like the ear canal, the Eustachian tube is made of two different parts, but in the reverse order.
The third closest to the middle ear is bony and about twelve millimeters long.
The bony part lies inside the temporal bone, just below the tensor tympani canal, and is always open.
The two thirds closest to the nasopharynx are made of cartilage and membrane and are about twenty four millimeters long.
The cartilaginous part is closed at rest and opens only briefly at certain moments.

cumleler.yazi: The point where the two parts meet is the narrowest part of the tube and is called the isthmus.

cumleler: In the ear canal the outer third was cartilage; in the Eustachian tube it is the two thirds on the nasopharynx side.

cumleler.yazi: The main muscle that opens the cartilaginous part is the musculus tensor veli palatini, the tensor of the soft palate.

cumleler: Like the tensor tympani, this muscle is supplied by the mandibular branch of the trigeminal nerve.
During swallowing and yawning it contracts, pulls on the cartilaginous wall and briefly opens the tube.
The levator veli palatini also helps open the tube as it lifts the soft palate.
In children with cleft palate these muscles attach differently, so the tube opens poorly and middle ear fluid is very common.

ogeler.metin: Equalizes pressure; if impaired, negative pressure
Clears secretions; if impaired, fluid builds up
Stays closed; blocks secretions and sound

cumleler: The Eustachian tube has three main functions: ventilation, drainage and protection.
Ventilation lets air enter the middle ear regularly and equalizes its pressure with the outside.
Drainage carries secretions from the middle ear to the nasopharynx through ciliated cells and muscle action.
The protective function relies on the tube staying closed at rest.
A closed tube makes it harder for secretions and microbes in the nasopharynx to pass into the middle ear.
It also keeps the person's own voice and breathing sounds from reaching the middle ear directly.
In a healthy ear, middle ear pressure is close to the outside pressure, and the tympanogram peaks near zero.
But the middle ear mucosa constantly absorbs the gas in the cavity.
By opening briefly during swallowing, the tube replaces the lost air and equalizes the pressure.
If the tube cannot open well enough, negative pressure builds in the middle ear and the tympanogram peak shifts to negative pressure.
The fullness felt in the ear as a plane descends is related to this; outside pressure rises, but the tube fails to open and equalize it.
Swallowing, yawning or chewing gum opens the tube and eases this feeling.
If negative pressure lasts a long time, the middle ear mucosa may start to secrete fluid into the cavity.
In this example, a child's right ear shows mildly reduced air conduction thresholds, while masked bone conduction is normal.

cumleler.yazi: The tympanogram is type B with a normal ear canal volume; this picture is consistent with middle ear fluid.

cumleler: The air-bone gap of about twenty five decibels comes from the fluid blocking the transmission of sound.

cumleler.yazi: As tube function recovers, the fluid often decreases, and the tympanogram may return first to type C, then to type A.

cumleler: The final assessment and the follow-up decision always belong to the physician.

ogeler.metin: Softer cartilage, weaker muscle in infants

cumleler: In children, the Eustachian tube is clearly different from the adult tube.
In infants the tube is about eighteen millimeters long, roughly half the adult length.
In adults the tube forms an angle of about forty five degrees with the horizontal plane.
In infants this angle is about ten degrees; the tube is almost horizontal.
The infant's tubal cartilage is softer, and the opening muscle works less efficiently.
The tube usually reaches adult length at around seven years of age.
A short, horizontal tube makes it easier for secretions and microbes in the nasopharynx to reach the middle ear.
Because the tube opens weakly, ventilation is poor and negative pressure develops more easily.
Large adenoid tissue in the nasopharynx can also narrow the tube opening and act as a source of microbes.
The frequent upper respiratory infections of young children swell the tube's mucosa and impair its function.
Together, these factors explain why otitis media, inflammation of the middle ear, is so common in children.
As the tube grows longer and steeper, middle ear problems usually become less frequent.

sahneler.baslik: A tube that won't open, or won't *close*

ogeler.metin: Fluid may build up in the middle ear

cumleler: Eustachian tube dysfunction can appear in two opposite forms.

cumleler.yazi: The more common form is a tube that cannot open well enough; negative middle ear pressure and a type C tympanogram are seen.

cumleler: The person feels fullness in the ear; if this lasts, fluid may build up in the middle ear.
Less often, the tube stays open more than normal; this is called a patulous Eustachian tube.
These people hear their own voice and breathing echoing loudly and unpleasantly in their ears; this is called autophony.
During tympanometry, deep breathing can produce ripples on the curve that are in time with respiration.
There is more than one method for assessing Eustachian tube function, and each has its own advantages.
In the Valsalva maneuver, the person closes the mouth and nose and gently strains to push air into the middle ear.

cumleler.yazi: In the Toynbee maneuver, the person swallows with the nose closed; this usually creates mild negative pressure in the middle ear.

cumleler: A change in peak pressure between tympanograms taken before and after the maneuvers shows that the tube can open.
Special tests such as sonotubometry and tubomanometry measure tube opening more directly, but not every clinic has them.
In routine practice in Türkiye, assessment is mostly done with tympanometry and these simple maneuvers.

sahneler.metin: When you see a type C tympanogram, ask the patient to swallow a few times and repeat the measurement. A peak shifting toward zero shows the tube can open.

cumleler.yazi: A tip from practice: when you see a type C tympanogram, do not write the result down right away.

cumleler: Ask the patient to swallow a few times and repeat the measurement.
A peak that shifts toward zero shows that the tube can open; this information is valuable in the report.
In children, crying and sniffing can also change the peak pressure, so measure during a calm moment.
The third of the Eustachian tube on the middle ear side is bone; the two thirds on the nasopharynx side are cartilage.
Closed at rest, the tube is opened by the tensor veli palatini muscle during swallowing and yawning.
The tube ventilates the middle ear, drains its secretions and protects it from the nasopharynx.
In children the tube is short, nearly horizontal and opens more weakly, so middle ear problems are more common.

sahneler.soru: Which is the main muscle that opens the Eustachian tube?
sahneler.aciklama: The _tensor veli palatini_ opens the tube by pulling on its cartilaginous wall during swallowing and yawning.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: Which is the main muscle that opens the Eustachian tube during swallowing?
The correct answer is C: the tensor veli palatini.

cumleler: This muscle is supplied by the trigeminal nerve; its function is impaired in cleft palate, so middle ear problems are common.
